One of the most powerful Qur’anic images of promise and warning on the Day of Resurrection is: “On that day you will be presented, and nothing about you will remain hidden. As for the one who is given his record in his right hand, he will say, ‘Here, read my record! I knew I would meet my reckoning.’ He will be in a life of contentment, in a lofty garden, with its fruit hanging near. ‘Eat and drink with pleasure for what you sent ahead in days gone by.’ But as for the one who is given his record in his left hand, he will say, ‘If only I had not been given my record, and had never known my reckoning. If only death had been the end. My wealth has done me no good. My power has vanished from me.’ ‘Seize him and bind him. Then burn him in Hell. Then thread him through a chain seventy cubits long.’” Qur’an 69:18–32.↩︎

The people of Medina came to be known as the “Ansar,” the Helpers, because they supported Islam from the time of the Hijra.↩︎

The name “Muhajirun,” the Emigrants, originally referred generally to the first Muslims who migrated with Muhammad to Medina after the Pledge of Aqaba. Later, “Muhajirun” and “Ansar” became fixed names used in Islamic history to distinguish the Muslims of Mecca from the Muslims of Medina.↩︎

Ibn Khaldun described analogy in legal reasoning as follows: “Many cases were not covered by established texts, so the Companions compared them with what had been established and attached them to matters explicitly mentioned in the texts, according to conditions that made the equality between the two cases or similar things valid. In this way it became highly probable that God’s ruling in both was the same. By their consensus, this became a legal proof: analogy.” Muqaddima, p. 817.↩︎
